query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding a refractory high-entropy alloy (specifically a WVTaTiCr-based coating) onto steel rollers or guide plates will significantly improve corrosion resistance to molten aluminum, thereby prolonging component service life under hot dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uncoated steel rollers/guide plates commonly used in hot dip aluminum plating lines
generation.intervention: Deposition of ~300–500 µm thick WVTaTiCr-based refractory high-entropy alloy coating via laser cladding at ~1.4–1.6 kW power and 8–10 mm/s scan speed
generation.conditions: Components continuously exposed to high-temperature molten aluminum baths under typical hot dip plating temperatures
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, refractory-enriched cladding layer with aluminum- and chromium-rich protective phases that act as diffusion barriers to molten Al
generation.mechanism: Refractory high-entropy alloys have high thermal stability and enhanced oxidation/corrosion resistance due to synergistic strengthening by multiple principal elements and protective oxide scales that impede aluminum attack
generation.predicted_outcome: Substantially reduced erosion/corrosion and longer service life relative to uncoated steel substrates under extended molten aluminum exposure
generation.baseline: Uncoated steel rollers in the same molten aluminum environment exhibit severe corrosion and short service life
generation.boundary: Limited direct data for molten aluminum environments; long-term performance depends on coating integrity, bath chemistry, and process parameters
generation.uncertainty: While initial oxidation and corrosion studies of WVTaTiCr coatings are promising, direct, prolonged testing in molten aluminum is still needed to confirm performance

falsification_experiment.design: Compare coated vs. uncoated steel rollers in a controlled molten aluminum bath at standard plating temperature, monitoring mass loss and microstructural integrity over time
measurements: Tensile or hardness tests of post-exposure samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated steel experiences corrosion and material loss similar to uncoated steel, or does not provide a measurable increase in service life, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. decision.trend: Early studies on NbMoCrTiAl (#PMC7513042) focused on enhancing high-temperature mechanical strength for refractory high-entropy alloys. Subsequent work on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (#PMC9955357) investigated corrosion resistance in a molten salt environment, establishing that these concentrated alloys can outperform conventional steels under intense corrosive conditions. More recently, research has emphasized protective multilayer or refractory-based coatings (e.g., WVTaTiCr coatings via laser cladding on steel substrates, #PMC10142552) to achieve robust barrier layers for corrosion and wear protection at high temperatures. However, direct evaluations in molten aluminum remain sparse, leaving open questions about the specific stability, interfacial integrity, and compatibility of these advanced alloys or coatings in prolonged contact with liquid aluminum.
decision.unsolved: Despite advances in high-entropy alloys and refractory-based coatings for high-temperature and corrosive media, the direct testing and long-term validation of these materials in continuous hot dip aluminum plating environments is still lacking. Materials that exhibit excellent performance against molten salts or high-temperature oxidation have not yet been fully evaluated in molten aluminum, where severe chemical reactivity and erosion pose unique challenges.
decision.lever: Laser-clad a durable refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoCrTiAl or WVTaTiCr-based) onto steel rollers or guide plates under a power of ~1.4–1.6 kW and scan speeds around 8–10 mm/s to achieve uniform, dense protective cladding layers of ~300–500 µm thickness.
decision.why: Because molten aluminum is aggressively corrosive, the most direct extension of current research on high-temperature HEAs and refractory-based coatings for harsh environments (#PMC9955357, #PMC10142552) is to apply a robust, oxidation- and corrosion-resistant coating onto existing structural steels. This approach avoids further composition changes while leveraging known benefits of advanced refractory high-entropy layers that have shown promising performance in other extreme environments (e.g., molten salt and high-temperature oxidation).
